question: to the Commission Arkadiusz Mularczyk (ECR) Subject:

The agreement on stronger air passenger rights confirms how important air transport is to citizen mobility and the functioning of the European Union’s single market. However, the dynamic development of airports also generates significant social, environmental and infrastructure costs, largely borne by local authorities. One example is Jan Paul II Kraków-Balice Airport, Poland’s second-largest airport and one of the fastest growing airports in Central Europe. The municipality of Zabierzów, the municipality of Liszki and the city of Kraków are facing increasing costs related to aircraft noise, necessary expansions of the road and public transport systems, environmental protection and spatial planning constraints resulting from the operation of infrastructure that is important at both national and European scale. 1.
Has the Commission analysed the impact that large airports have on the financial situation and quality of life of neighbouring municipalities?

Does the Commission intend to propose a dedicated financial mechanism or programme under the future EU Multiannual Financial Framework 2028–2034 to support municipalities and regions bearing above-average operating costs of the TEN-T network’s aviation infrastructure, particularly through financing investments to reduce noise, improve public transport, develop road infrastructure and protect the environment? This mechanism would allow for a fairer distribution of the costs and benefits of developing European transport infrastructure and would strengthen public acceptance for further development of strategic airports.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (28.8.2026) The Commission has not undertaken such analyses. The effects that airports may have on their surroundings are, however, reflected in several strands of EU legislation. This includes Directive 2002/49/EC on environmental noise1, Regulation (EU) No 598/2014 which sets rules and procedures with regard to the introduction of noise-related operating restrictions at Union airports2 and a growing body of air quality, environmental assessment and nature legislation. This allows the Commission to monitor environmental and infrastructure-related impacts of airport activity. The detailed assessment of local social, planning and budgetary consequences for municipalities remains, under the principle of subsidiarity, primarily a matter for national, regional and local authorities. In any event, several studies show that air connectivity enabled by airports is key for growth, jobs, social cohesion and vital for EU regions3. In 2025, a report on the impact of Polish airports on regions found that Kraków-Balice airport had a direct impact of PLN 470,7 million on the Małopolska region’s economy and an induced impact of PLN 240 million and 1.700 jobs, bringing a gross value added of PLN 1,56 billion to the Polish economy4. The Commission has not proposed a dedicated financial mechanism for this purpose. Under the next multiannual financial framework, support for such investments may be available through different EU funding programmes in line with the objectives and rules of the relevant funds. Any supported project will need to comply with relevant EU environmental legislation.
